whatever the row count, and K3 already verifies up to 255 lookup rows in one
frame. A tree spends those rows on alternatives instead of depth.

A request that reaches its `deadline_ms` while a rank is disconnected
answers `504 deadline_exceeded` with `missing_rank`. When the engine has
latched a failure other than a disconnect (a rank or adapter protocol
failure), every request answers `503 engine_failed` naming the status until
the ranks restart or reset; the API no longer reopens a failed engine for
each request.

- **Path.** The receiver offers its addresses and the sender takes the first that
  connects: cisco (`10.10.201.x`), then the CRS804 (`10.10.100.x`), management,
  LAN and tailscale. The summary line names the path used, so a copy that fell back
  says so.
- **Integrity.** Every chunk carries a SHA-256 computed from what was read at the
  source and checked on arrival before it is written. A file reaches its final
  name only when all its chunks have arrived, so a failed or killed copy leaves
  no partial file behind and the previous version intact. The check covers the
  read and the network. It does not read back what the disk wrote.
- **Memory.** Files of 64 MiB or more use direct I/O and are preallocated, so a
  bulk copy does not fill the page cache on a Spark during a run.
- **Priority.** Both ends run at nice 10. On cisco0 TCP sits in the default queue,
  so RoCE keeps its share of the port and the priority classes stay ahead of it.

- `SparkWeightdManifestLoad` allocates the range, group and spine tables, so
  it is a startup call. On success the caller owns them until
  `SparkWeightdManifestDestroy`. On failure the function frees them itself
  and leaves the struct zeroed.
- Status: `NOT_FOUND` for a missing file. `PARSE_ERROR` for a non-regular
  file, a bad magic or version, a non-zero reserved word, a zero-length,
  oversized, out-of-pack or overlapping range, a repeated kind in one group,
  a short file, or bytes after the last record. `CAPACITY_EXCEEDED` for zero
  ranges or more than `SPARK_WEIGHTD_RANGES_PER_EXPERT_MAX` ranges in one
  group, besides the range-count bound.
- Groups are sorted by (layer, expert) and the ranges of a group by kind.
  `SparkWeightdManifestFind` is a binary search over the groups.
- `SparkWeightdManifestSpineSlice` translates a pack slice to its compact
  spine offset with a binary search over the spans, O(log N). The slice must
  lie inside one spine span, that is, touch no expert range; otherwise
  `NOT_FOUND`. `spine_allocation_bytes` includes the alignment padding
  between spans, so it can exceed `spine_bytes`. For a private spine,
  `SparkWeightdLazyPackCreate` allocates it plus 255 bytes and rounds the
  base up to 256, so a slice keeps its pack alignment in device memory.
- `SparkWeightdManifestLayerChunks(manifest, chunk_bytes, first_layer,
  layer_count, &chunks)` counts the distinct `chunk_bytes`-aligned chunks that
  the expert ranges of layers `first_layer .. first_layer + layer_count - 1`
  touch; layers with no ranges count 0.

The indexer pool score (`Glm5NextPoolScoreKernel`) ran one block per row and
local pool. Each block rebuilt the pool's softmax-mixed key, which depends
only on the sequence and the pool. It then reduced 32 heads one after
another through `LmBlockSum`, about 130 block barriers for 4,096
multiply-adds. Its cost grows with context, since a wave scores every pool
that came before it. Waves of 64 rows or more now run
`Glm5NextPoolScoreRowsKernel`: one block takes 32 pools and 16 rows, builds
each pool's key once, keeps a row's queries in registers and gives each warp
four heads. The head score replays the block-sum tree exactly. Each 8-lane
group first sums its four elements in the tree's first two levels, then
does three width-8 shuffles, and the four group sums combine in the
eight-warp order with the zero-valued warps added in. On one GB10 a
2,048-row wave takes 2.6 ms against 30.8 ms at 16K context, and 10.1 ms
against 130 ms at 64K. The scores are bitwise equal, including -inf and
unwritten entries (`tests/test_glm5_next_pool_score_cuda.py`).

- The client collects fds only from its first `recvmsg` of a frame. Later
  reads of the same frame use `recv`.
- The control buffer has room for at least 253 descriptors, the Linux
  per-message limit, so every fd the kernel delivers is seen, even past the
  protocol cap. A truncated control message (`MSG_CTRUNC`) fails the read.
- Each fd is made close-on-exec. Fds beyond the caller's capacity (64
  through `SparkWeightdClientExportExchange`, 2 for a lazy attach) are
  closed and fail the read.
- Any failure closes every fd received so far and returns `IO_ERROR`, so the
  caller never gets a partial set. Failures include over capacity, a
  truncated or malformed control message, an expired deadline or failed
  `poll`, and EOF or a receive error before the frame is complete. The
  exchange then closes the client socket.
- The caller then checks the fd count against the frame.
  `SparkWeightdClientExportBatch` requires the request id, the batch offset,
  `batch_count <= 64` and `batch_count` equal to the fds received. A lazy
  attach requires exactly one fd for each of `mesh_ready` and
  `pool_fd_staged`. A mismatch closes every fd and the socket. The export
  returns `SCHEMA_ERROR`, or the header validation error when the header
  itself is wrong; the lazy attach returns `SCHEMA_ERROR` in both cases. A
  batch is exactly what its frame declares, or nothing.
- `SparkWeightdAttachImportMap` (`runtime/spark_weightd_attach.c`) closes
  each chunk fd right after `cuMemImportFromShareableHandle` succeeds. A
  failed import closes the batch's remaining fds.

The gain is at the first divergence. With one chain the expected accepted
tokens are the sum over depth of the path survival; with a tree it is the sum
over every node of its path survival, so a second candidate at depth 1 with

the unified design gives the same order. That is the target to measure

**Pair-first routes.** A route with the `pair_first` bit carries two payloads
in one publication (`SPARK_WEIGHTD_MESH_PAIR_FIRST_BYTES(group,pair)`). The
group bytes go to every peer of the sender's parity, into the sender's own
slot half. The pair bytes go to the partner (`rank ^ 1`) over the pair link,
one piece per segment of the partner's parity, each into the slot half of the
sender of the other parity (`SparkWeightdMeshPairFirstArea`). Every other peer
gets only the tail. Two collectives use it:

1. `SparkWeightdClientConnect`, then `SparkWeightdClientAttachLazy` with a
   120 s timeout. `tools/weightd_warm.c` makes the same call. The client maps
   the daemon's mesh memfd at a 64 KiB-aligned fixed address
   (`SparkWeightdMapSharedFd`).
2. The tool requires a non-null `mesh_send_buffer_addr` and
   `mesh_send_buffer_bytes == SPARK_WEIGHTD_MESH_REGION_BYTES`, then creates
   the CUDA context.
3. It calls `cudaHostRegister` on the whole region three times: with
   `cudaHostRegisterPortable | cudaHostRegisterMapped` (the flags
   `SparkTpDeviceCollectivePrepareReceiveBf16` uses), with
   `cudaHostRegisterPortable`, and with no flags. After each success it prints
   the `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` result and unregisters.

- Background work runs only when no interactive request is queued or running on the lane, one job at a time, and gives way between waves.
- The bound on an interactive request is one background wave. Where one wave is too long (GLM 5.3 Full at long context), background commits stop at a context limit until a wave can be aborted.
- The keeper never activates or swaps a model. An entry for a model that is not resident waits.
- A commit the client asks for at a session's start is that session's own work and runs in the interactive class. Only the keeper's own work is background.
- A prefix is computed once. A request whose prefix another request is already computing waits for it to be published, so eight subagents that start together on a cold opening cost one prefill, not eight.
- A saved prefix is restored, never recomputed. On Kimi K3 a restore is 200–500 times cheaper per token than prefill.
- When the budget is short, openings are kept first, then packs, then sessions ranked by the recompute seconds they save per gigabyte. Entries are dropped from the other end.

recepit-verified shard-by-shard; vetting = provenance pinned +
full-receipt hash + quality gate on first serve). Our packers
REPACKAGE — format conversion into stagepacks, TP/PP sharding, scale

quantization exists, serve the publisher's native precision (BF16
packs fit the fleet: Qwen Flash bf16 = 84G/rank at TP4) rather than

future precision change means adopting a NEW official/vetted source

- One deadline covers a whole exchange, write and read. It comes from the
  caller's timeout, or `SPARK_WEIGHTD_CLIENT_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_NS` (10 s) when
  the caller passes none.
- `SparkWeightdClientReadAll` reads exactly the frame size. An expired
  deadline or a failed `poll` returns `BUSY`. EOF or a receive error before
  the frame is complete returns `IO_ERROR`: the daemon is gone or broke
  protocol.
- `SparkWeightdClientExchange` closes the client socket and sets it to -1
  when any step fails, including a header or request-id mismatch. Later
  calls on that client fail with `IO_ERROR`, and the client object does not
  reconnect.
- This is the client half of the crash semantics in the perf notes: once the
  daemon is lost, the next exchange fails, and so does every later call on
  that client.

The spine is the sorted exact complement of the expert ranges. It includes
headers and padding and has no digest of its own, so the loader validates the
pack identity before publishing a pointer. Compact spine offsets keep each
source offset's alignment modulo 256. `SparkWeightdSpineLoad`
(`runtime/spark_weightd_spine.c`) copies only the spine spans when the pack
has a valid verify-once receipt (below). Without one it streams the whole
pack through a 1 MiB buffer, SHA-256 hashing all of it while copying only
spine bytes, and records the receipt. With a per-chunk (non-pooled) map, do
not map complement spans at their pack VA: small padding gaps would pin
nearly every expert chunk. A pooled map already covers the whole pack, so
there the spine is read in place (below).

  partitioning, dependencies, collective identity, credits and progress in
  common topology code. Model hooks supply stage math and boundary geometry.
- **I36 — Select the collective algorithm by regime.** Common collective code
  chooses from degree, operation, datatype, logical batch, payload bytes and
  the measured crossover profile, as in README's regime table: one-round
  direct all-to-all for latency-bound payloads, reduce-scatter plus
  all-gather over slice routes for bandwidth-bound sums, and the pair-link

  hardware) is a deployment input and must not change which algorithm runs.

  order. Prove overlap on the execution timeline, not from asynchronous API

  across ranks, steps and generations. Workspaces and credits remain valid
  through GPU and transport completion. Measure exposed communication, rank
  imbalance and weight reuse lost through splitting; splitting is not free.
- **I38 — Qualify each topology.** TP16, TP4xPP4, PP16 and any other

- **I39 — Functional and performance verdicts are separate and mandatory.**
  A correct but slow driver is functionally qualified and performance-lagging.
  An incomplete or numerically wrong driver fails functionality regardless of
  speed. Neither state is “done.” Required evidence cannot be waived by paperwork.
- **I40 — Numerical gates test the real model.** Use pinned references and
  qualified tolerances for prefill, decode, mixed batches, long contexts,
  restored state and each topology. Repeatable nonsense is still wrong.
  Acceptance tools must reject bad/nonfinite values and propagate failures.
- **I41 — Separate timing phases.** Report load, prefill, TTFT, warm decode and
  batch tails separately. Seed a complete reusable cache entry, verify its hit,
  and benchmark decode on the persistent engine. HTTP wall time is not pure
  decode time. Report per-sequence latency alongside aggregate output tokens/s.
- **I42 — Compare matched workloads.** Match context, occupancy/traffic, timing
  boundaries, weight precision, speculation and hardware. Current GLM targets
  are non-speculative. Cite and verify community measurements before treating
  them as baselines; record uncertainty and normalization assumptions.
- **I43 — Normalize bytes and hardware honestly.** FP8 at half a 4-bit rate can
  be comparable only under an explicit bandwidth/traffic assumption. Account
  for actual weights, scales, expert traffic, cache traffic and quantization
  work where available. Four times the nodes must not disappear from the comparison.
- **I44 — Prove the GLM targets.** Establish a numerically correct TP4 baseline
  approaching measured sustainable memory roofline. Target TP16 at 3.5 times
  matched TP4 throughput and a filled TP4xPP4 pipeline at approximately four
  times TP4 serving capacity. These are acceptance targets, not claimed results;
  queued requests alone are not demonstrated capacity.
- **I45 — Hill-climb from evidence.** Profile the actual critical path, optimize
  the measured bottleneck, then repeat unprofiled measurements and numerical
  checks. Record bandwidth efficiency, exposed communication, occupancy,
  variability and regressions. Summed overlapping kernel times are not elapsed time.
- **I46 — Evidence is reproducible and scoped.** Preserve commands, source/build/
  pack identities, hardware/network topology, budgets, queue attempts, outputs,
  latency traces and verdicts. Protect credentials and private infrastructure
  details. A merge, compile, local smoke test or zero sanitizer errors cannot
  stand in for distributed functional and performance acceptance.
- **I47 — Reviews enforce these invariants.** Developer PR feedback identifies
  the violated rule, the existing common primitive to use, the required change
  and the behavioral evidence needed. Record GLM fixes and measured lessons
  so subsequent drivers follow the proven path rather than inventing variants.
- **I48 — No comments in code.** Put rationale, design explanations and
  implementation notes in documentation and PRs. Express the implementation
  clearly through names and structure. Tests verify executable behavior and
  contracts, never the presence or wording of comments. Do not restore or add
  a comment to satisfy a test; fix the test.

The first campaign is GLM-5.3 Flash TP16 (`qualification/ab/fleet/glm53flash_w1.json`):

- **Expansion copies the residual into the streams.**
  - `LmHcExpandStreamsKernel<HIDDEN>`: one element per thread, stored to all
    four streams (GLM 5.3 Flash, Motif 3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash).
  - `LmHcExpandFlatKernel<STREAMS>`: one element of the flattened streams
    per thread (HY4). Its launch covers `STREAMS * width` threads.
- **Mixes.**
  - `LmHcSite<HIDDEN, P>`: an eight-block cluster splits the flattened
    streams. The family's policy `P` declares the gates and the combination
    (`Glm5NextHcPolicy`, `MotifHcPolicy`). The same kernel collapses the
    streams with the new pre weights and snapshots them for the post update.
  - `LmHcSinkhornMixes<STREAMS>` (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash): eight per-warp
    partial dot products a row, from `LmHcSinkhornPartialKernel` below 32
    rows or `LmHcSinkhornPartialStagedKernel` from 32 on (four rows a block,
    eight from 512). The staged kernel copies each 256-element step of the
    mixer weights and the block's rows into shared memory three steps ahead
    and splits the 25 tasks over two thread groups, so its accumulators stay
    in registers; thread `t` of a group still sums elements `t`, `t + 256`,
    ... in order and the warps reduce as before. The two give the same bits
    (`tests/test_dsv41_hc_mix.cu`).
    `LmHcSinkhornKernel` then sums the partials in warp order and writes
    `pre = 1 / (1 + exp(-u)) + eps`, `post = 2 / (1 + exp(-u))` and a
    source-major combination: a softmax over each row from its maximum plus
    eps, a column normalisation, then `iterations - 1` row and column
    normalisations, each `+ eps`. The collapse runs separately, in
    `LmHcCollapseKernel` or fused into the consumer through
    `LmHcCollapseElement`.
  - `LmHcMix<THREADS, STREAMS, MIXES, WIDTH>` (HY4): no combination. It
    writes the pre weights `sigmoid(u) + eps` and, with `2 * STREAMS` mixes,
    the post weights `magnitude * sigmoid(u) + eps`, and it collapses the
    streams in the same pass. Up to `LM_HC_MIX_SPLIT_ROWS` (16) rows it
    splits each dot product over 256 lanes (`LmHcMixDotKernel`, then
    `LmHcMixRowKernel`). Above that it runs four rows a block
    (`LmHcMixKernel`). `LmHcMixPartialBytes` sizes the split's buffer.
- **Post updates.**
  - `LmHcPostKernel<STREAMS>` (HY4): `bf16(fma(post_s, out, x_s))`, with no
    combination.
  - `LmHcPostBf16Kernel<STREAMS>` (GLM 5.3 Flash): post weights and a
    source-major combination rounded to BF16, and each term rounded.
  - `LmHcPostF32Kernel<STREAMS>` (Motif 3): a target-major combination in
    FP32 with one rounding, one row per `blockIdx.x`.
  - `LmHcPostF32SourceMajorKernel<STREAMS>` (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash): the same
    FP32 formula over a source-major combination, one row per `blockIdx.y`.
- **The reference set is test code.** The single-block kernels used by the
  DeepSeek V4.1 Flash layer test and `build/libdsv41_flash_kernels.so` live
  in `tests/cuda/dsv41_flash_hc_reference.cuh`. Their block sums differ from

The indexer pool score (`Glm5NextPoolScoreKernel`) ran one block per row and
local pool. Each block rebuilt the pool's softmax-mixed key, which depends
only on the sequence and the pool. It then reduced 32 heads one after
another through `LmBlockSum`, about 130 block barriers for 4,096
multiply-adds. Its cost grows with context, since a wave scores every pool
that came before it. Waves of 64 rows or more now run
`Glm5NextPoolScoreRowsKernel`: one block takes 32 pools and 16 rows, builds
each pool's key once, keeps a row's queries in registers and gives each warp
four heads. The head score replays the block-sum tree exactly. Each 8-lane
group first sums its four elements in the tree's first two levels, then
does three width-8 shuffles, and the four group sums combine in the
eight-warp order with the zero-valued warps added in. On one GB10 a
2,048-row wave takes 2.6 ms against 30.8 ms at 16K context, and 10.1 ms
against 130 ms at 64K. The scores are bitwise equal, including -inf and
unwritten entries (`tests/test_glm5_next_pool_score_cuda.py`).

- The client collects fds only from its first `recvmsg` of a frame. Later
  reads of the same frame use `recv`.
- The control buffer has room for at least 253 descriptors, the Linux
  per-message limit, so every fd the kernel delivers is seen, even past the
  protocol cap. A truncated control message (`MSG_CTRUNC`) fails the read.
- Each fd is made close-on-exec. Fds beyond the caller's capacity (64
  through `SparkWeightdClientExportExchange`, 2 for a lazy attach) are
  closed and fail the read.
- Any failure closes every fd received so far and returns `IO_ERROR`, so the
  caller never gets a partial set. Failures include over capacity, a
  truncated or malformed control message, an expired deadline or failed
  `poll`, and EOF or a receive error before the frame is complete. The
  exchange then closes the client socket.
- The caller then checks the fd count against the frame.
  `SparkWeightdClientExportBatch` requires the request id, the batch offset,
  `batch_count <= 64` and `batch_count` equal to the fds received. A lazy
  attach requires exactly one fd for each of `mesh_ready` and
  `pool_fd_staged`. A mismatch closes every fd and the socket. The export
  returns `SCHEMA_ERROR`, or the header validation error when the header
  itself is wrong; the lazy attach returns `SCHEMA_ERROR` in both cases. A
  batch is exactly what its frame declares, or nothing.
- `SparkWeightdAttachImportMap` (`runtime/spark_weightd_attach.c`) closes
  each chunk fd right after `cuMemImportFromShareableHandle` succeeds. A
  failed import closes the batch's remaining fds.

The gain is at the first divergence. With one chain the expected accepted
tokens are the sum over depth of the path survival; with a tree it is the sum

the unified design gives the same order. That is the target to measure
against, not a multiple.

branch loads the fixture cubin,
checks the reported layout, refuses bindings and a wrong-sized block, and
reads back a launch. It also creates, launches and destroys a kernel with

and reads every word back, and refuses a block 4 bytes over the limit.
`SPARK_DEVICE_PROPERTY_SHARED_ADDRESS` is always set. The backend sets

from `NV0000_CTRL_CMD_GPU_GET_ID_INFO_V2`. GB10 reports it. A discrete GPU
does not, so on one the backend makes no claim of host-coherent memory,
as the CUDA backend does from its integrated flag. The backend adopts no
foreign memory or queue. Adopting one of the device's own live queues works
on every backend: the device layer finds the handle in its own list of
queues by comparing pointers, never by reading through the handle, and
hands back that queue as a borrow. The caller gets the same record, so the
owner's sequence numbers and capture state apply. A release while borrows
remain only returns a borrow, so the owner and the adopter may release in
either order, and the last release destroys the queue. Any other handle, a
freed queue's included, goes to the backend and is refused. This lets a
runner adopt its execution stream the same way in the nvrm flavour, where
the stream is a device queue, and in the CUDA flavour, where it is a CUDA
stream. A queue the backend owns is never captured into a graph.

The spine is the sorted exact complement of the expert ranges. It includes

token per rank. At ~100 Gbps line rate (12.5 GB/s) with recursive
doubling (log2(16)=4 hops), the wire time is microseconds — BUT the
kernel-launch + sync overhead per reduce is ~20-50 µs, so 184 reduces ≈
4-9 ms per step JUST in launch overhead. That overhead, not bandwidth,
is why TP16 didn't beat TP8.

Events are 32-byte marks carved from a pooled host allocation. Recording
one is a queue operation that releases a timestamped copy of the event's
next generation 16 bytes into the mark, then the queue's fence, then an
unsigned 64-bit maximum of the generation into the mark's first word. The
event completes when that word reaches the generation, by which time its
queue has passed the record; a later record that finishes first is never
undone by an earlier one. A queue waits on an event by acquiring the
mark's first word at or past the generation, so waits between queues
need no host round trip. Elapsed time is the difference of the two
marks' GPU timestamps.

- Launches go into one serial compute encoder per command buffer, and copies
  and fills into blit encoders in the same buffer. Buffers use Metal's tracked
  hazards, so a launch, a copy and a launch on one queue see each other's
  writes in order (`TestKernelOrdering`).
- Command buffers hold unretained references; the device layer's stamps keep
  every bound buffer and kernel alive until the work that uses it completes.
- A host callback runs on the queue's worker thread after everything before it
  completes, and the queue holds the command buffers queued after it on the
  host until the callback returns, so the callback has the same ordering as
  `cudaLaunchHostFunc`.
- An event completes with the command buffer that records it. A queue that
  waits on an event that has not completed holds its later command buffers on
  the host, and the recording queue's worker commits them when the event
  completes. Event timestamps are the command buffer's `GPUEndTime`.
- The GPU never waits on an event or a callback. macOS aborts a command buffer
  that waits on the GPU for about five seconds
  (`kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorTimeout`: an M4 passes a 4 s wait and
  aborts a 5 s one), and an aborted buffer faults the device. Cross-queue waits
  used to be `encodeWaitForEvent` on an `MTLSharedEvent`: on 2026-11-17 the M5
  Ultra's Qwen3.8-27B engine waited that way on its KV copy-on-write fence for
  about 5 s, the step was aborted, and every request failed until the engine
  restarted. `TestLongHold` holds one queue behind a callback and another
  behind the first queue's event for 6 s.
- A failed command buffer marks the queue and the device faulted; the next wait
  returns `IO_ERROR` with Metal's error text, and every later device call fails
  (as on the other backends). The serving adapter prints that text when a step,
  keep or reset wait fails.
- A faulted device cannot serve again in that process, so the serving
  adapter's snapshot then reports its lane fatal
  (`SPARK_MODEL_DRIVER_DEGRADED_LANE_FATAL`, as after a failed streamed
  prefill). residentd reads the snapshot whenever it delivers a failed
  completion, whether the adapter refused the submission or completed it with

  failing every later request (I11). On the fleet the node agent starts a
  fresh engine on a later pass of its loop, and the API's requests wait for

Every CUDA hyper-connection kernel lives in these two headers. A family
selects its variant by name and template arguments and defines none of its
own. The variants stay separate because their arithmetic differs: merging

- `H` is the ±1 Sylvester Hadamard matrix of order 128, applied blockwise.
- `W_inner[r, c]` is `LUT[state]`. The state for tile position `t` is the 16
  bits of the tile's bit stream that end at bit `(t + 1)·K`, tail-biting.
  The stream is the tile's uint32 words (little-endian pairs of the int16
  words), MSB first.
- Position `t` maps to a row-major tile element through the tensor-core
  permutation (32 lanes × 8 values).
- `LUT` is the 65,536-entry table for the linear's codebook: `mcg` (marker
  tensor `.mcg`, multiplier 0xCBAC1FED), `mul1` (`.mul1`, 0x83DCD12D), or
  3INST without a marker. The tool refuses a table whose sha256 differs from
  the pinned value that was checked against exllamav3 on all states.
- K is read per tensor from the trellis width, so mixed K3/K4 needs no map.

A row's result depends only on its own inputs and on which projection kernel

the GEMV computes every row with the same sequence of operations whatever
its pass size, the tensor-unit kernel tiles rows in 16 or 32 with identical
arithmetic for each row (the two tile heights give the same bits), and its
split count depends only on the projection's shape.

independence`, with and without row tiles and row-exact frames). So with row
tiles every row of every step up to 64 rows has the bits of a one-row step:
every batched sequence decodes exactly its solo tokens, and a verify frame
computes each row exactly as plain decode does while reading the weights
once. With the GEMV family one or two sequences give exactly the solo
tokens, three to 64 give the same tokens as one another but not the solo

(`row_exact`) runs the GEMV passes so that it stays exact.

Trust boundary. The seal is an unkeyed checksum: it catches a torn or
hand-edited receipt, not a forged one. Anyone who can create files as the
loading user or root can mint a receipt, and could equally rewrite the pack,
so receipts add no trust beyond that uid. A receipt vouches for the file's
metadata, not its bytes. Changes that bypass the filesystem's ctime are not
seen: media corruption after verification, raw block-device or debugfs
writes, or root moving the clock and restamping. Run
`weightd_receipt verify <pack>` to re-hash a pack when its bytes are in
doubt. A writer that already holds a shared writable mapping is covered by
the `O_DIRECT` verification pass: it writes dirty pages back and
write-protects them, so the writer's next store updates ctime. The receipt
also binds `st_dev`. On a node where device numbers can change across a
reboot (several NVMe drives probed in varying order, or device-mapper), the
first load after the reboot re-verifies once.

**Slot ring depth (IPC ABI 17, record magic `MESH0010`).** A rank has four
slots a band, eight half positions, where ABI 16 had two. A pipelined round
may then publish three pieces before its first arrival and keep three in
flight (`SPARK_WEIGHTD_MESH_PIPELINE_DEPTH`): a rank publishes piece `k` after
it has read piece `k - 3` from every peer. A peer that has published piece
`k - 3` has read piece `k - 6`, so the half position piece `k` reuses, that of
piece `k - 8`, is free on every rank. A whole-slot round shares its slot with
the sequence four later; inside a pipelined round that is piece 3 after a
whole-slot round that ended just before piece 0, and piece 3 goes out only
after piece 0 has arrived from every peer, which a peer publishes only after
reading that round. With two slots the shared slot was two sequences later, so
a round had to read piece 0 from every peer before it published piece 1, and
the wire stood idle for one combine kernel at the start of every round.
